Aerobic efficiency

pace at HR 135–155

Pace at a fixed heart rate is the cleanest read on aerobic fitness. It has to be compared on flat runs only — your latest quarter averages 12.1 m of climbing per km against 1.6 at your best, so the raw number can overstate the decline. Corrected for terrain the drop is 21 s/km, not 59.

Where your running intensity actually sits

The long run has gone backwards

runs of 15 km or more

6 long runs in twelve months, and the last one was 2 July. Phase 2b opens on 28 September expecting 22–26 km. From a current ceiling of 11.2 km that is a jump you cannot make in one step, and the marathon behind it needs 30 km+.

Load you have not budgeted for

seasonal pattern

Ice hockey ran 3–5 sessions a month across the season, then stopped completely in April. If the season restarts on the same calendar, roughly 23 high-intensity sessions land straight on top of Phase 2b and the taper — and your plan does not mention hockey at all.

Recovery & sleep

the one measurement problem

Recovery is the good news, with one caveat about how it is measured. Garmin reports a resting heart rate even on nights you did not wear the watch, derived from daytime readings — and those run about 15 bpm high. Read naively, your resting HR looks like it sits around 62. Counting only the 65 nights with real overnight data, it is 47 and has been all along. The apparent trend was measuring your watch habits.

You are blind on 81% of nights

HRV, body battery, sleep score and much of training readiness all derive from overnight wear. At 19% coverage most of your recovery data simply does not exist — and the gaps get silently backfilled with worse numbers. This is the cheapest fix on this page: wear the watch to bed.

What to change

in priority order

  1. Put a floor under the week before raising the ceiling

    Three runs every week beats four-then-one. Your 49% week-to-week variation is doing more damage than your average mileage suggests. Target a floor of 20 km, every week, before chasing a 35 km week.

  2. Rebuild the long run from 11 km, not from the plan's 22

    Add roughly 2 km a week: 13, 15, 17, 19. That reaches the low end of the Phase 2b requirement by late October without a doubling jump, and it is the same base the marathon needs afterwards.

  3. Add one 1 km repeat session a week — it is literally the race

    6–8 × 1 km at target race pace with short recovery. Start it now: at 137 days without genuine speed work, the first few sessions rebuild a capacity you already had in April, not a new one.

  4. Log the strength and station work, or plan around its absence

    Right now the two are indistinguishable in the data. If you are lifting, record it so load and readiness mean something. If you are not, that is the larger finding — the station half of the race is untrained with 15 weeks left.

  5. Decide about hockey before October decides for you

    Either budget 4–5 sessions a month into the peak block and cut running intensity to match, or sit out the first half of the season. Both work. Being surprised by it in November does not.

  6. Wear the watch overnight

    Zero training cost, and it turns 81% of your recovery data from guesswork into measurement — right as the load starts to climb.
